decision.reason: As noted in the prior parent objection, the paper does not merely cite McNiel and Fleeson (2006) as background; in the Introduction (lines 271-290 and 341-367), the authors cite McNiel and Fleeson (2006) and McNiel et al. The authors critique the small sample size (n = 45) and within-subject design (order and carryover effects) of those two studies and explicitly design Studies 1 and 2 with between-subjects manipulations, larger samples, and measures of both positive and negative affect to re-test whether counterdispositional behavior increases negative affect (reporting in the Study 1 and Study 2 Discussions that their stronger test replicated the positive-affect benefit and absence of a state-by-trait negative-affect cost). Shipped row 881 is Fleeson, Malanos, and Achille (2002, DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.83.6.1409), which did not measure negative affect and is a different original study.

decision.reason: In Section 1.7.2 (External funding effect), Section 2.8.2, Section 3.3.2, and Section 4.2 (Extensions), the authors formulate and empirically test Hypothesis 7 across Studies 1 and 2 (combined N = 706), testing whether donors prefer a charity whose overhead costs are covered by another donor over a charity where donations pay for overhead when cost-effectiveness is held constant. In Section 4.2, the authors explicitly state that Hypothesis 7 acts as a conceptual replication of Gneezy et al. [16] (Gneezy, Keenan, & Gneezy, 2014, DOI 10.1126/science.1253932), contrasting Gneezy et al.'s between-subject design with their own within-subject design. The only shipped row (row 826) is Baron and Szymanska (2011, DOI 10.4324/9780203865972-24), which is a different original work that did not test externally funded overhead.
